[h1] Risk of rain 2 is the kind of roguelike where you wanna have just one more quick run before bed but end up playing till dawn. [/h1]

[b] Visuals: [/b] 
The art style is easy on the eyes early on, but as the run continues and your screen starts to fill with clutter, the diarrhoea christmas lights at later stages can be seizure inducing.

[b] Story and Setting: [/b] 
RoR2 doesn’t hold hands and guide you through its story because honestly there is not much story going on here. There is rich lore to explore for people who want to.

[b] Music: [/b] 
The lo-fi melody perfectly fits the perilous environment and matches the gameplay with synced rhythm and tempo. Sound design is good too.

[b] Gameplay and progression: [/b]
Drop into a planet, kill monsters, get money, buy items. Rinse and repeat until you become powerful to one shot God himself. Fast paced with constant running, jumping, sliding and juggling between primary weapon, secondary weapon, abilities and equipment. In each run the difficulty increases over time, which is an innovative approach to deal with difficulty. The roster is filled with unique characters who each have their own gameplay mechanics, making the game feel completely different. 
Most items can be obtained by completing specific challenges. You can also unlock game modifiers to make the game easier or more difficult to your liking. The challenges are one-of-a-kind, and the rewards are meaningful enough to keep players interested.

[b] Game time: [/b]
There is no limit. It stops being fun when you decide so.

[b] Online: [/b]
There is co-op to enjoy with friends and difficulty scales with the number of players. And if you have no friends, rest assured because all achievements are attainable through single player.

[b] Bugs: [/b]
No bugs or technical issues.

[b] PC Requirement: [/b] 
Without a decently powerful PC the game faces severe lags and occasional crashes in long runs where you loop multiple times and a million things are happening in the background. Lowering graphical settings can help to an extent.

[b] DLC: [/b]
Survivors of the Void DLC adds excellent new characters, stages, items,  enemies and alternate endings.

[b] Price: [/b]
Worth every penny.

[b] My only problem with the game is it doesn’t have a save system. Once you start a run, you will have to see it through to the end. I want to be able to stop at any stage and continue from there later on. I don’t always have hours required to do multiple loops in one sitting. Although there is a mod for saving, I would love a native option. [/b]

[b] Rating: [/b] 
The Devs are continuously supporting and updating the game which is commendable. The community is very active and you can add tons of community made [b] mods [/b] to breathe new life into your game. 
I highly recommend it. [b] 10/10 [/b]

A game about surviving on an alien planet where the local wildlife has collectively decided you are a walking loot crate. Developed by Hopoo Games, a studio that clearly asked the question: “What if dopamine addiction was a game mechanic?”

In Risk of Rain 2 you crash-land on a hostile planet and must fight through increasingly angry wildlife while collecting items that stack so hard they eventually turn the laws of physics into a polite suggestion.

You start as a normal survivor with a pistol.

Ten minutes later you are:

Firing 300 homing missiles per second

Causing chain lightning across the continent

Summoning orbital bombardments whenever you trip over a rock

Accidentally killing God because you picked up your 47th goat hoof

The core gameplay loop is simple:

Land on planet

Kill everything

Open chests

Become a walking war crime

Die instantly to something you never saw

Every run begins with optimism and ends with a lemurian breathing on you for 0.3 seconds and deleting your entire existence.

But that’s okay, because the real game is the items.

You see, items in Risk of Rain 2 stack.

Not politely.
Not reasonably.

Stacked like a Soviet apartment block made entirely of cocaine.

You get one syringe: faster attack speed.
You get ten syringes: you become a living minigun.
You get fifty syringes: your GPU files for political asylum.

Some items trigger other items which trigger more items, creating a cascading chain reaction that eventually looks like:

“Enemy hit → missile → explosion → lightning → fireworks → orbital laser → nuclear winter.”

At this point the screen is less of a video game and more of a weather event.

Now let’s talk about difficulty scaling, also known as “the game quietly loading a shotgun while you’re having fun.”

The longer you take, the stronger enemies become.

Meaning the game gently encourages you to move faster… until it becomes a frantic sprint through levels while screaming:

“WHERE IS THE TELEPORTER”

Meanwhile the timer ticks upward and the enemies evolve from:

Cute lizard
to

Angry lizard
to

Laser lizard
to

God’s personal hate mail

The bosses are equally fair and balanced.

Sometimes you fight a giant stone titan with laser eyes.

Other times the game spawns fourteen of them because you had the audacity to enjoy yourself.

And then there’s multiplayer.

Multiplayer in Risk of Rain 2 is a beautiful cooperative experience where you and your friends work together to survive.

By which I mean:

You steal every item you see while pretending it was an accident.

Friendship ends the moment someone grabs the Legendary Chest.

By the end of a run everyone has become a different type of natural disaster.

One friend is a lightning storm.
Another is a missile platform.
And one poor guy is still holding a revolver because the loot goblins got there first.

Eventually you either ascend to godhood or die to a jellyfish.

There is no middle ground.

But despite the chaos, the soundtrack—composed by Chris Christodoulou—is phenomenal. It perfectly captures the feeling of:

“Floating peacefully through space while committing industrial-scale violence.”

In conclusion:

Risk of Rain 2 is a beautifully designed roguelike about stacking items until the game engine begins to cry.

It’s fast.
It’s chaotic.
And it’s one of the few games where becoming a demigod still isn’t enough to survive a mushroom field.

10/10.

Would crash-land again.

I believe that the core of what makes a rogue-lite addicting is the power fantasy. When the RNG hits just right during a run, you become a God... and becoming a God is fun! Risk of Rain 2 understands this concept so incredibly well. 

In other rogue-lites, a good run means you feel powerful. In this game, you have the capability of becoming so insanely overpowered that you can barely even comprehend what is happening. Hundreds of enemies will spawn only to be instantly killed with a casual glance in their direction, exploding in a fountain of coins. On your tenth loop, you become essentially omnipotent - flying around the map at mach speed, thoughtlessly burning everything in your path as you stack another teddy bear on top of the pile and put on your 10th pair of red-tinted glasses. Until finally, like Ozymandias, your empire collapses in an instant when you greedily stop to scratch your nose, atomized into a million pieces by a random flaming jellyfish.

In RoR2, chasing that power fantasy dragon is so addictive on its own, but this game also happens to have the added benefit of featuring extremely engaging combat, interesting enemies, intense boss battles, awesome level design, a ton of fun items, a diverse cast of playable characters, multiplayer, challenge modes, and to top it all off... what I would consider the greatest video game soundtrack of all time. The music is just so incredible that I can't really put it into words.

Risk of Rain 2 is hands down my favorite rogue-lite, and one of my favorite games ever.

After 800 hours and completing all achievements for this game, I feel like it's time to write this.

You will hate this game, and then come to love it, and then hate it again, and then go back to loving it. You will go through every single emotion, every stage of grief, the highest of highs and lowest of lows playing this game, struggling at this game, and trying to improve at this game until it etches itself into you like the microplastics in your blood stream. And once it gets it grip on you, it won't let go. You're gonna keep coming back to this game. It won't matter why. Maybe you meshed well with similar games that allow for different play styles. Maybe you're too stubborn to let the game knock you down after losing, maybe it's because games have gotten too stale and that this is your last reliable source of pure, no nonsense gameplay. Even when you think you're done, you're not. Maybe there's a new update and you wanna take a gamble at how broken it is. Maybe one of your friends suggest you two play a run together like two crabs in a giant bucket. Maybe a mod releases that just let's you PLAY AS A TANK. 

I keep coming back to this game, more so than any other game I've played in my entire existence. Very rarely can a game like this feel as fresh on run 1 as it would on run 1000. I'm writing this after completing a monsoon Artificer run when most of my runs have been on rainstorm. That run in particular felt like one of the hardest challenges I've ever had to do, and vastly different from any of my autopilot huntress runs. 

I hate this game, and I love this game. I hate how this game has consumed me since I first game it an honest attempt at 4 years ago, yet I love how games like this can just exist. It's a game that will ruin slower paced games for you. It's a game with the potential of forming the strongest of bonds with other people. It's a game that will teach you how to get good at games. It's a game with a soundtrack made by someone who thinks he's the shit and has the evidence to back that up. It's a game that goes on sale for $8 that I put 800 hours in without even touching eclipse and having barely dipped my toes into modding.

It's a game.
Not a sad imitation of a movie
Not a glorified storefront or slot machine (although gambling is still present)
It's just pure, unrestricted fun

This game combines so many attributes of what one could consider a fantastic video game.

Controls? Tight.
Soundtrack? Banging.
Characters? Diverse.
Items? All unique.
Levels? Beautiful.
Difficulty? Punishing.
Hotel? Trivago.

Okay, time for the serious part. With over 550 hours under my belt, a 100% in achievements, and calling it one of my favourite roguelites ever, I come back to this review to cement my opinion further.

An incredibly unique gameplay loop reinforced by good traditional roguelite aspects make this such an engaging and rewarding game to play. I absolutely love just jumping into a run, surviving against crazy odds and using my knowledge to prevail and become more powerful than you could imagine in a video game.

Lets get down to the F.A.R.T.S Score!


F for Feel: S. Smooth movement, combined with fast-paced action, varying enemy types, powerful bosses and elite enemies aimed to exploit your weaknesses, leaves this game never having a dull moment at all. If you crave high-octane killing action and becoming an all-powerful god, this is the game for you. But only if you earn it! (or get lucky enough :P)

A for Art: A+. My favourite game that goes for the "simple but impactful" design. Colours are vibrant, but textures aren't very detailed - a lot of things are mostly one or two colours, but that's all this game needs. With so much happening on-screen, the developers really nailed a balance of detail and simplicity to make sure that it never feels messy even though there are piles of dead corpses on the ground and particle effects everywhere. It's just really coherent! There is also a grand sense of scale, the world extends for ages beyond the playable area, making you really feel lost on an alien planet. The enemy and character designs all fit well together and are really unique as well.

R for Replayability: S-. With many items and unlockables, there always seems to be a new goal in mind for a completionist. And if you have done all that, then there's Eclipse mode for the hardcore player. Or simply trying to go for a high score is very fun. Or using scrappers to control your build and harness as much power as you can from the game. Or this. Or that. You get the point. There's always another way to play the game!

T for Tunes (OST): S+. Oh my god, what can I say about Chris Christodoulou's soundtrack. It's my favourite of all time, thats for one. The music absolutely binds this game together. From an intriguing and dark intro cutscene track, to the more upbeat and encouraging menu theme, to a spacious, explorative stage theme, to a boppin' electronic boss theme to a fast-paced prog-metal boss theme, TO A STRAIGHT UP JAZZ-METAL FUSION FINAL BOSS THEME WITH SAXOPHONES, back to touching, thought-provoking acoustic guitars and pianos. What the hell. This soundtrack is an complete rollercoaster trip to another universe and back. Chris is an absolute musical genius and I love him to bits. Thank you so much for making this game whole. Absolutely cannot praise it enough.

S for Story: A-. There is some story here, and it's pretty encouraging and relevant when you think about it. It ties in with the previous game mostly. Its essentially a rescue mission from the gang's previous encounter with a demigod - and this time,  the god is even more pissed. Reading the logbooks also provides some really nice worldbuilding for this universe, set in the not-too-far future. Explore and see what you can piece together, its more than you might think!

Final Score; S. Top-tier roguelike gaming right here folks. It has it all. Read my first statement above, because it still holds true 100% to this day.

The original Risk of Rain was one of my first experiences in PC Indie Gaming, and it left quite an impression on me. From its stylistic character design, to the 2d side-scrolling ability spam fest, and an ending with music so beautifully appropriate it ended up permanently etched into my mind. This game has received a lot of bad publicity over the last couple of months due to the Seekers of the Storm DLC that was launched way before it was ever ready, but if you're new to the game, I'd still highly recommend playing Risk of Rain. Before the DLC, it was one of my all time favorite games ever; in fact I think it's one of the best rogue-like games I've ever played.  
It's been a few months into the bug-fixing and whatnot, and at the time of writing I think the game is about as stable as it was pre-DLC (with maybe a few more enemies clipping through walls). The original content and fun-factor is still there for new players, and survivors of the void is still a solid DLC for those who want to play more. If you get super into it like I have been, I still wouldn't purchase the seekers of the storm DLC just because they are going to be updating the added survivors and they'll probably continue to re-balance and re-work items since the game is still a bit too easy with seekers items enabled; give it a couple more months and wait for it to be fully baked, and in the mean-time there's still a whole lot of content to enjoy if you're a new player. The base game comes with almost every survivor (except for 5 spread across 2 DLCs), and they're all exceptionally fun to play. Base-game items and difficulty is generally very challenging; especially when you're a new player, it can be difficult to understand how to most effectively deal damage and heal but playing usually makes you get into the hang of it, and if you really want to get into the nuts and bolts of how to play well and beat higher difficulties (Eclipse 8), you can just look at the wiki to read about proc coefficients (basically the chance to proctor a chance based item off of an attack), but none of that is at all necessary to enjoy the fun of the game. 
Anyways, play Risk of Rain! It's cool and neat and I've sunk 400 hours into it so I'm pretty sure you'll get enough content to justify the money you'll spend on it!

Okay, let's throttle off the Praise and actually give you an idea what you are getting into with this game.

So, if you have already played the first game this part is mostly pointless to read, but to anyone new to Risk of Rain, it works like this:

You spawn into a map, and there are chests and interactables scattered around the map to pick up. Most of it is purchased with gold that you earn killing the enemies that spawn gradually here and there. Everything you pick up collects as passive bonuses. These are all basic things you see in most roguelikes. Area transitions involved activating a Teleporter that spawns a boss and several small minions to challenge you before you make it to the next area, and staying in that teleporter's radius (visual AoE, you need to be near it to charge it). It won't finish charging and enemies will keep spawning while the boss is alive.

Here's where things really twist: As you play, you have a timer and a Difficulty Gauge underneath. The longer you survive in Risk of Rain, the higher the difficulty gets. Each rise in difficulty means more abundant enemies, tougher enemies, and higher chances to encounter "Elite" monsters that deal more damage and have special properties (As of now there are Fire, Ice, and Lightning). This means that as you keep going and grab more things in an attempt to grow as powerful as you can, you are also constantly facing bigger and tougher swarms of enemies popping up and trying to end you. This means it's a race to get as many items as you can find, activate the portal, kill the boss, and move on as far as you can go, before you inevitably get completely swarmed by 7-8 Elite Golems that all have their laser sights on you at once.

This make the game extremely addictive in nature and incredibly fun to play with your friends. Most of what was in the original 2D Risk of Rain has been implemented while remaining true to it's origin, but now in 3D, with many extra things added to spice things up.

Another important note I think anyone considering this game should know is the Devs are extremely in touch with their community at this time, and through both their Risk of Rain 2 Discord channel and their forums are actually actively looking over observations and suggestions from their player base. This review is being typed out right after their latest patch, build #3731106. Looking over this patch, a majority of it is changes made either by community suggestion or something reported by them. This gives me a lot of hope for the future of the game so far, and I really appreciate this kind of relationship with Developers. Thank you for your hard work thus far, Hopoo!

So, if you haven't guess it by now I highly recommend this game to anyone (who enjoys surviving until they get ridiculously overwhelmed and die horribly to a Kamekaze Elite Jellyfish swarm, like me).

[h1] Enter the Loop at Your Own Risk [/h1]

As a newcomer to the Risk of Rain series, I was attracted to Risk of Rain 2 because of its co-op online, horde-like shooter structure with a fresh 3D perspective compared to its predecessor's 2D format. Just like other horde-like games, it follows the "loop" design of kill mobs, collect loot, defeat the boss, and rinse-repeat.

The gameplay is simple, intuitive, yet challenging all at the same time. The gameplay is brutal, but fair. It is challenging but not in a frustrating way. I just want to play more. It is the kind of challenge you can appreciate and learn from your mistakes. I'm new to rogue-likes-lites and I was able to solo for more than an hour. 

As far as unlockables, there are six characters to unlock, four zones, and 99 items with more on the way. Items that you collect along the way are adorned on your character like trophies. Despite all the unique passive abilities you get from each item, I want to see more items with cool powers and abilities that I can summon. For top-tier players, they may feel content-starved. Personally, I feel there is enough content here in Early Access to keep you coming back for more. 

Playing with keyboard and mouse and the controls feel slick, snappy, precise. Items and abilities complement one another, making for a perfect formula for mayhem. Aiming and gunplay are precise and accurate. Enemy hit box is fine-tuned. Using terrain adds another layer of dimension to combating enemies.  Discovering new items and experimenting with them is extremely fun. And using them on enemies is even better. One of my favorite items is the black hole. Needless to say, it speaks for itself. 

Visually, Risk of Rain 2 sticks to what its good at, and just like the original it sports a very similar coat of aesthetic that is hauntingly beautiful and minimaliistic. The game runs extremely well @ 3440x1440 on my ultrawide and doesn't miss a beat. As you well know by now, Risk of Rain 2 is in 3D. Unlike its 2D predecessor, the third-person perspective and added dimension does not take away from what makes RoR great. Enemy attacks and projectiles now come from every direction instead of a lined approach, which changes things up for the series.

The soundtrack is superb. If you like listening to soundtracks from "Deep Rock Galactic", "Blade Runner" or the movie "Drive", your ears will be pleased. The soundtrack is calm and soothing to the ears against all the chaos on the screen. There's also some rock, too, that goes well with some intense play sessions.

Online multi-player consists of co-op online featuring quick play or simply hosting a game and inviting your friends. It has a [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198002524847/screenshot/923708812833647767]Multi-player Lobby.[/url] Some of the issues I experienced were some rubberbanding and the "Unknown Lobby ID" or "Invalid Lobby ID" when trying to use QuickPlay. Other than that, it has been pretty smooth for an Early Access game. 

Another feature that I really liked was the option for players to vote on difficulty level in the lobby. In the past, I have found too many games fall into the trap of map selection based on difficulty, which can really split the community. On the other hand, this may cause some players to quit because the difficulty level is too hard. One draw back is that it runs on peer-to-peer online connection. I had a few great "monsoon" difficulty runs end because the host quit. 

My one caveat with the online portion is that any player in co-op is able to click on teleport prematurely which transfers the entire group to the next area before looting everything. This causes some players to miss out on collecting the remaining items on the map. On easy difficulty, this isn't much of a problem. But on harder difficulties this can present an issue. 

Some players have complained about the visibility of the teleporter. I do not think it is all that bad. The teleporter visibility and randomization varies. Sometimes, I would go rounds finding it rather too easily. Once in a while, it feels like it doesn't even exist on the map.

Another issue are how boss drops are distributed. The boss will drop at least one item per player. Sometimes, the boss will drop more items than there are players. In my experience, some players would grab more than one item or all of them, possibly to troll others in the group or they just do not want to share. Also, because the items drop very close to each other, it is easy to grab more than one boss drop item by mistake. 

The levels are hand-crafted like the original. While they are designed well, there is not enough randomness. The teleporter is randomized, but you can expect the rest of the levels to be the same.

It was not until recently that I got into rogue-likes, thanks to some Steam friends. Usually, I would play co-op, horde-like games such as Deep Rock Galactic (excellent game btw), Vermintide 2, Helldivers, and so forth. If you like any of those games and you like some rogue-likes, or you are at least open to them, I think you will probably like Risk of Rain 2. I was not too fond of the original RoR, but I felt right at home with RoR2. It is like a love letter to co-op, horde-like gamers.

Risk of Rain 2 was a pleasant surprise. Rarely do I instantly like a game this much within the first hour. Its simplistic and elegant design has a mild complexity when it comes to its challenging gameplay. It consists of smart design that allows any type of player to jump right in, so long as you have the patience for it. 

In the future, I would like to see more rogue-like-lite titles become 3D games. As long as it makes sense and works well with the gameplay style. Hopoo Games has shown that indie titles such as RoR can be a 3D title and still retain all the aspects that made the original a great, fun game.

RoR2 is in Early Access and kicking with overwhelmingly positive reviews and it is well earned. The developers plan on adding more characters, bosses, items, a true endgame boss, and a true ending when the final product releases. Game modifiers that can be found in the world will be coming soon as well. Furthermore, I want to commend Hopoo Games for doing the "Buy One, Get One Free until 3/30" promotion. [h1] A Case Study in Beautiful Suffering [/h1]
Damn near the 200-hour mark, and I find myself reflecting on this game the way one might reflect on an ancient text: with reverence, confusion, and the growing suspicion that my death is a core game mechanic, not a consequence.

Risk of Rain 2 is a procedurally generated fever dream engineered by a team of developers who clearly passed both calculus and therapy with flying colors. It's a masterclass in ludonarrative alignment: the story is told not in cutscenes, but in how loudly you scream when a blind pest punts you off a cliff at 38 minutes into a god-tier run.

Every death is an unscheduled performance review. The game doesn’t ask, “Are you ready?” It says, “We’ll find out.” You don’t play Risk of Rain 2—you participate in a hostile merger between your self-esteem and randomized item drops.

[h1] Pretty Praise [/h1]
The characters? Legends. The gameplay? Crack. The difficulty? Feels like the devs coded in personal vengeance. And just when you think you're built different, the game reminds you: you’re built like a limp baby arm.

The itemization loop is nothing short of alchemical. Characters scale from squishy interns to demigods of destruction in a ballet of synergy, probability, and hubris. And yet, no matter how strong you get, the game evolves with you—an adaptive ecosystem of things that want you dead and have the tools to make it happen.

[h1] A Roguelike That Rogues My Life [/h1]
My favorite moments? The deaths. Not even kidding. You think you’re a god with 17 ukuleles and 3 goat hooves, then a jellyfish sneezes in your direction and suddenly you’re a speed bump on the lunar highway. It’s humbling. It’s poetic. It’s pain in stereo.

Do I desire more content? Naturally. But that craving exists not from deficiency, but from excellence. What’s here is complete. It’s curated chaos. It’s interactive poetry for masochists and min-maxers alike.

[h3] Final analysis [/h3] 
11/10. Would get obliterated again.

I've been waiting till I got all the achievements to write this review, and well today is the day. 
Long story short, this game is fucking amazing. Buy it, get some friends to buy it and you will have a wonderful time. This game is a 10/10 in every category and everyone needs to experience it. But, personally I feel this game isn't deserving of such a short review so here we go.

-Gameplay and Characters
The initial gameplay is just amazing and borderline addicting. It, of course, is a roguelike so you will be trying and dying and trying again but that death is almost never frustrating, especially in the early game. This is because you will be getting item after item, working to unlock everything you can and every run feels like you are making progress even if you didn't get much further than the last run. And the main gameplay elements feel amazing because of the great cast of characters. They all feel unique with their own advantages and disadvantages and the feeling of finally unlocking a new character is unmatched by any other roguelike. In other games, you may unlock another character but many times they just feel like a reskin of the first character with a different weapons but here each character plays so vastly different from one another it is incredible. The cast of characters range from a gunslinging dude in a space suit, to a lizard dog thing that shoots acid at people. Some of my favorites include Mercenary - a samurai who while very tough is just fun to play - Captain - who has an amazing primary shotgun but is bogged down by lack of mobility - and Loader - who is basically spiderman mixed with the prawn suit from subnautica. The best part is that no character feels really bad. Some are worse than others to me but it allows everyone to find someone they enjoy playing and stick with them. Plus they all have more unlockable skins and abilities which makes you want to play them all. 

-Atmosphere music and Graphics
The atmosphere in this game is top fucking notch. Each area is distinct with a certain style that is only helped by the amazing score. When I first heard it, I likened it to a mix of celeste and subnautica. An oddly calming and alien blend that I know see and distinctly risk of rain. The music in the final level is downright a masterpiece,  and after playing the first game, I can say that the music is some of my favorite rivaled only by celeste and the doom games. The graphics likewise, are amazing. Compared to the low res pixel art of the first game, the models here looks so damn nice. The characters and items fit perfectly in these truly breathtaking levels. Scorched Acres, Titanic Plains and Sundered Grove are just beautiful and a joy to explore and look at. Then you have the more alien worlds like Gilded Coast and the Bulwark Ambry which give you such a good sense of atmosphere and make me wish I could just teleport there and listen to the soundtrack while reflecting on life as a whole. 

-Level design 
The interesting part about this game is that while it is a rogulike the levels aren't completely random. They are always pretty much the same with some areas not being available sometimes with bridges being out or tunnels being blocked. This does wonders to the gameplay because you can become familer with the stages while also having variety from run to run. Plus there is the fact that there are an average of 2 different locals you can visit for each of the 5 stages. This does lead to some flaws with some being better than others but on the whole it is very nice and I hope to see more stages added to each level. As for each level, They are all very good but have a few flaws. Some are much harder to navigate if you character doesn't have any mobility and some are harder to find the teleporter, but on the whole they are all quite good. 

-Enemies and Bosses
The enemies in this game are just great. You have certain enemies like beetles and hermit crabs that pose no threat but on the opposite side of the spectrum you have the most terrifying enemies like parents, greater wisps and elder lemurians who I still have nightmares about to this day. These enemies all spawn in different ratios and certain enemies only spawn on certain levels which adds to the variety and uniqueness of each stage. Having different types of enemies makes the player think but there aren't too many overall types as to overwhelm the player. The extra variety comes in the form of elites which can make even the most trivial enemies forces to be reckoned with. Then there are the bosses which come in 10 forms and spawn as teleporter bosses or as regular enemies in later stages. They are all unique and pose different challenges. There are also more formal bosses like the Alloy Worship Unit, Aurelionite and the Final boss. The first 2 are just reskins of other bosses but the Final boss is something special. I would say he might be the weakest part of the game but that is only because I have only fought him a few times. When the 1.0 update first came out, he was almost impossible on monsoon but now I feel like he is a little more balanced. Again I would have to fight him more to develop a final opinion but as for a final boss, he fits quite well.

-Difficulty
The challenge this game poses can be quite daunting at first but I feel like on the whole it is perfect. To start there are 3 difficulties to choose which affect enemies, regen and other factors which lets players choose how they want to play but there is also the time mechanic. The longer you take on a stage the harder the game gets. This means that you have to balance your time between looking for items and beating the stages and progressing. This makes for a great difficulty curve and I would say the only spike in difficulty is on stage 5. It is insanely hard and will be one of the biggest roadblocks in any run. But there is also more choice in difficulty, because you can end the run by beating the final boss or looping which sends you through earlier stages with much much harder enemies. I prefer to loop because it allows for crazier god runs but overall it is amazing to have so much choice.

-Fun with friends
Before I wrap this up I want to touch on how amazing this game is with friends. Most of my playtime was with my friend who had most of the stuff unlocked already and it made the game easier to get into. Now playing with 2 or 3 other people is just great. Failing over and over again is much better with friends, and it works just great here. The only issue is that it is much much harder in multiplayer but I would prefer that to it being a complete cakewalk. 

-Final Thoughts
Overall this game has been a joy, and though I have most things completed I still want to keep playing. I may try it with mods or might just stick to vanilla and see how good of a run I can get. I would also like to point out artifacts which I am very mixed on. They can make the game hectic and amazing but sometimes command just breaks the game to a point where is gets stale. That is to no ones fault but my own but I can't help but feel like I'm cheating. Hell, I didn't even beat the final boss on monsoon without artifacts till the time I'm writing this review. Anyways, I am extremely excited about the future of this game with more updates and DLC and I hope the next one will be able to rekindle that magic of unlocking a new character for a first time. And if you made down here without buying the game, what is wrong with you?!

I remember a lot of apprehension when Risk of Rain 2 was announced. It wasn’t unwarranted, either, as the jump from 2D to 3D has been dire for more than a few franchises. I wasn’t super hot on the original Risk of Rain either, owing to how sloggy the combat could be if your build didn’t keep up with the hordes. But all those concerns melted away in my first few minutes with the game. Risk of Rain 2 benefits so much from the move to 3D that it’s almost hard to believe it started as a side-scroller, with free movement and open arenas allowing you so much more control over encounters. And I can only assume it’s going to get better from the handful of foes and levels it has now.

The story in these games is always a pretty big question mark, but the premise at least is simple enough. You’re some kind of space badass, landing on a bizarre alien world full of things eager to teleport all the way over to kill you. The only way to progress through these realms of slaughter is to find and power up a teleporter, which of course will attract the attention of things far worse during the charging phase. On a happier note, the planet is dotted with mystical shrines, drones in need of masters, and cases full of suspiciously powerful items, all of which can enhance your survivability if you can wrest enough coins from your foes to pay for them.

At this precise moment, Risk of Rain 2 is a loop of six levels, each a wide-open space of fields, cliffs, walkways, ruins, and other features to explore. The map itself is always the same, save for minor differences like some doors and caves being open, but the layout of loot and the location of the exit teleporter is always different. You are free to explore to your heart’s content as enemies teleport themselves into your vicinity to murder you, but just as in the first game the difficulty rises as time passes. The main challenge of the game, then, is balancing your exploration for more powerful gear against the need to press on as your foes become stronger and more numerous. Once again, this is a balance that will take time to learn, and may end with you dead in the very first stage a few times as you seek to find it.

The big difference between the first and second games now is the pace of the action. In Risk of Rain you often found yourself corralling foes into a stack to whittle down, boxing in enemies and chewing through them gradually. Part of the reason for this was your low movement speed and lack of mobility options in platforming. All that is out the window now, and not just because of the addition of a third dimension. Relative movement feels so much faster here, with a dedicated sprint button and more dramatic movement abilities for the different classes. Items that add additional jumps are also pretty common drops, but more importantly enemies can no longer box you in. You’re free to circle around foes, weave through crowds, and retreat in any direction if things get too intense. You have to stay in the vicinity of the teleporter to charge it but that’s still a sizable arena to work with.

For the most part, the grinds against enemy health bars are gone as well. There are certainly some enemies that need further adjusting but the overall experience feels balanced more for cutting down big groups in a hurry. This is facilitated by the builds you can get going, featuring powerful pickups that conditionally enhance your damage or add leaping electrical attacks or explosive effects, all of which can be stacked with themselves. They say it right on the store page, they want you to exploit these items, creating builds that will tear through your foes like some kind of super-science reaper. These items will be familiar to fans of the first but it’s easier to get a build rolling in this one, possibly due to your greater relative power compared to your foes.

There are six classes to unlock and use in the game now, from the familiar shootyman Commando to the nimble Huntress with her homing bow to the absolutely mad techno-magician Artificer. More levels and classes are coming prior to the full launch early next year, as well as the game-altering Artifact system from the first. Right now you can enjoy some wonderfully chaotic drop-in multiplayer (which works like a dream compared to the first game) and daily challenges, the staple of modern roguelikes. All you really need is that core loop of looting and shooting, though, because it’s absolutely sublime here. I never expected Risk of Rain 2 to outperform the original so completely, but the move to 3D has treated it incredibly well. For wild arena combat and fast-paced adventuring, this one is hard to beat.

Risk of Rain is a cult classic. It has a very distinct pixel art style, a fantastic electric guitar lead soundtrack and lots of quirky items and alien monsters. Risk of Rain 2 transitions the game to a 3D third-person shooter and looking back at the original, the transformation is amazing. The pixel art sprites have become distinctively animated critters that puke psychedelic particle effects in every direction. The levels have gone from tunnel-like procedural platforms to hand-crafted, themed environments big enough for new players to get lost in. Some of the original characters have not been slated to return yet however it's important to remember that characters that worked well in 2D may not work so well in 3D.

The mechanics of the game are exact but vaguely explained: you'll need to spend some time discovering them or look for a guide or the wiki. In essence it's a bit of a speed running roguelike game. The longer you linger in the levels, the harder the game gets. Each stage has a teleporter that you must charge to reach the next. Activating the teleporter triggers a boss fight but the teleporter only continues to charge while you remain near it and you cannot proceed until the boss is dead. Along the way you get items from chests and vending machines, earning the required cash by killing monsters or pickups. Spend too long and the game will get too hard to continue. Go too quickly and you may find you don't have enough items to fight the monsters.

At the moment there's 5 main maps on a semi-randomised loop. Item and monster spawns are also randomised between hand placed spawn locations. There's a good amount of content to unlock: hundreds of items, a bunch of characters with more on the way, challenges to complete to unlock additional skills for each character and a daily 2 stage time challenge mode. One of the latest additions are unlockable relics which modify the game in extreme ways and can be combined to create a unique experience. This game also works on Steam Link and features coop multiplayer.

RoR2 is one of those games you can buy any time you want. It has co-op, but you don't need it to play, it's just as good SP. The graphics have a timeless cel-shaded look, so it's never going to look dated. This one's all about the gameplay. And as a roguelike/lite, you don't need to have a lot of time available to sink into it all in one go. If you buy it, you will likely put a ton of time into it, but each session doesn't have to last that long (maybe an hour once you get decent at at).

Why should you buy it? Well, it's my personal favorite roguelike, just barely edging out Binding of Isaac due to its more interesting cast of characters. And, like BoI, it's a game that appears on the surface to be a demanding bullet-hell that requires twitch skills, but after playing it for a while, that turns out to be mis-judging the book by its cover. It's actually more of a thinking game. Learning how the game's mechanics work leads to a mind-over-matter situation where you're able to put your knowledge into practice and turn what seems to be very difficult at first into something surprisingly easy -- as long as you make good strategic choices. Also, don't be scared that the game's difficulty ramps up over time, because learning to make good exploration and item choices means that your character grows in power faster than the enemies, and the clock becomes meaningless. It's not there to make the game punishing, it's there to require you to learn the game's mechanics. And once you do, it will feel like that scene in the Matrix where Neo suddenly realizes what he's capable of.

So this game is FINALLY out.  Well, out in early access anyway.  It's been a long wait, and I gotta say, it's been worth it.  Granted, it has some flaws... which are kinda big.... but for this most part, it's excellent.

This is essentially the natural evolution of the first game.  Instead of trying to transform the gameplay too much and replace entire mechanics or do things like that, they seem to have taken the approach of "if it aint broke, dont fix it".  They take everything that's good in the first game, and drop it in here.  This rather forms the core of the whole experience.  If you liked the first game at all... you're gonna love this, because it's more of the same, except way better.

If you havent played the first one, the whole thing is a fairly simple idea.  Being a roguelike, your goal is simply to explore each level, find the exit, and defeat the level boss.  All the while, you search for items to grab in order to build up your character in various ways.  

But RoR has never really followed the other traditions of the genre.  Gone are the room-based levels, replaced with enormous sprawling freeform zones.  You also dont roam around clearing areas of enemies as you do in most of these games.  Enemies constantly spawn.  What's more, they spawn NEAR you.  You'll see crab monsters burrow out of the ground, or golems assemble themselves in front of you.  The enemy assault never stops, and so neither does the action (most of the time).  What's more, the enemy appears in massive numbers.  10 foes at once?  Hah!  That's nothing.  Try 50!  Complete with elites mixed in, powerful versions of normal foes with some funky abilities added to them.   In addition, each character has not only a normal attack, but three other abilities that each operate with cooldowns... a concept very rarely seen in this genre.

All of this leads to a game with a very different feel from the rest of the genre.  That was the case with the original RoR, and that's the case here.  But here, we also have the jump to 3D, and that improves everything.  The original game could be oddly methodical... even with a bazillion enemies at once, combat could be a little slow in a way.  It's hard to explain, but if you try that game out or even just watch some videos of it, you'll see what I mean.  But here, that has changed.  Not only does your character just move alot faster, but the 3D nature of the game means that enemies can appear anywhere, and attack from any angle.  Dodging and positioning yourself properly becomes even more important with so much chaos going on.  Learning to keep track of all the lunacy around you is important as well, as is choosing the targets for your various attacks, so as to defeat enemy groups as fast as possible.  Combat is fast and visceral, and involves lots of crazy movement and leaping around.   I actually think this game may have the best combat and action of the entire genre, and that's not something I say easily.  It's THAT good.

What's more, there's good variety here.  Each character has their own unique skillset, and they're differentiated quite well, never feeling like clones or slight variations of each other.  Items are also well varied, meaning that each run will actually feel different from the last, adding even more to that "one more run" feel of the game that makes it so addictive.  Even though you collect so many items over the course of a run, each one still feels meaningful and exciting to find.  There is alot of RNG in finding items... the game isnt big on things like shops, for instance, to give you the opportunity to make choices... but when you DO have choices to make (usually from the funky triple gizmos that offer a choice of 3 items), the choices feel like they have a solid impact on your run.   And there are loads of fun items to find here.  This element of the game never gets boring.

Same with enemy designs.  Yeah, you're going to see the same foes over and over, but that's fine.  They're very well done, and generally work well in the context of the game's horde-focused combat.  Each enemy has it's own unique style of attack, and learning what each foe can do is quite important.  And none of these guys ever feel unfair or broken for the most part.  Nor do they seem like a waste of space.  You know, the sort of enemy that's so weak and easy that it makes you wonder why they are even in the game.  None of that here.

Same with the bosses.... with one exception.  The Stone Titan is... broken, at best.  With a literally undodgable deathray attack, you *must* dive behind cover to avoid massive damage.  What's that?  It showed up in an area with no cover?  Well, tough.  Fight it anyway, you dont get a say in the matter.  As I'll say about ANY game in this genre, undodgable ANYTHING is pretty much the cardinal sin.  Fortunately this is the only foe capable of it... but it doesnt make it any less of a problem.  It's a real chore to fight that guy, and the frequency with which he shows up is a problem... there just arent that many bosses right now, so expect these fights to repeat FREQUENTLY.  

A much bigger problem is the teleporter.  You must find this thing to complete each stage.  It is where you spawn the boss and begin the "charging" event, a chaotic battle that marks the end of the level.   That idea is fine.  What ISNT fine is the teleporter itself.  It's nigh-invisible half the time.  It blends in with everything.   Sometimes it is halfway stuck inside a big rock or something, making it even harder to spot.  Or there's the awful swamp level, where it's damn near impossible to see most of the time and can even appear submerged in water.  I often find myself restarting a run simply because the swamp level showed up, because I just cant be bothered to deal with the tedium of searching for a nearly invisible exit.

Speaking of tedium:  Holy hell do I hate the process of unlocking stuff in this.  Now granted, I say that with literally every game in the genre.  I never have, and never will, like unlocking stuff.  I know that gamers these days seem to need an endless string of "goals" to work towards, or they get bored (thus the existence of achievements) but for a player like myself, it's just a pointless irritation.  I'll likely be downloading a completed save file the moment I can find one, rather than put up with the bloody unlock process.  I dont play games like this for achivements and unlocks, and this game is worse than most about that.  If you've played Isaac, think of some of the more RNG-based, super-irritating unlocks found in that game.... yeah, there's alot of that here.

This game isnt about the unlocks anyway.  It's about the sheer fun and the variety and challenge.  It just does not get old.  Not only are you going to have an absolute blast, but you'll keep having an absolute blast even after 100 hours of playing it, just like with the first game.  Even in it's early access state, and even with the occaisional wonky flaw, RoR 2 is a masterpiece.  With boatloads of content, the best combat ever, and incredible variety, the fun just never stops here, and you'll always be wanting to do just one more run, just one more....

Just pick it up, and see for yourself how brilliant it is.

Now if you'll excuse me, I have to go back in and fight more monster swarms.  The 7 runs I did just before this wasnt enough.

When Covid locked everyone inside I stopped seeing my dad over the weekends for four months. We had played Risk of Rain back when I was seven, so when he found out that a second game had been made, he bought himself and I a copy so that we could play well we were both stuck inside. He passed away five months ago, from a heart attack. Now when I play this game all I remember are all my fond memories of unlocking characters and reading through logbooks. just a month after his death, I bought a copy for my cousin who had been almost as close to him as I had been, since her parents weren't the best around, and now I had spent nearly as much time playing this game with my cousin as I had with my dad. we still miss him dearly, but all of the fond memories lighten the pain.

 ( Also, me and my cousin just bought the new DLC and it's dope as hell! Fun times all around. )
